contributions.headingText: Type B3 thymoma is a thymic epithelial tumour predominantly composed of mildly or moderately atypical polygonal tumour cells, accompanied by small numbers of non-neoplastic immature T cells.
Not recommended: atypical thymoma; well-differentiated thymic carcinoma.
Type B3 thymoma is typically localized in the anterior (prevascular) mediastinum; ectopic occurrence is rare {25740445}.

One third of patients are asymptomatic. Others have chest pain, cough, dyspnoea, or superior vena cava syndrome. In the International Thymic Malignancy Interest Group (ITMIG) cohort {25616178} and an independent meta-analysis (see #14398Table 5.01), myasthenia gravis and other autoimmune disorders occur in 40–50% and about 5% of patients, respectively {12459627; 16731193; 25616178; 31982129}.

Imaging

The imaging features overlap with those of other thymoma types {18514124}, but type B3 thymomas are more likely to be of higher stage and show higher FDG uptake {21623235; 23446204}.

In the ITMIG cohort {25616178} and an independent meta-analysis (see Table #14398), type B3 thymoma accounts for 16–21% of thymomas. In these cohorts, the median and mean ages are 52 years and 55 years (range: 8–87 years), respectively. There is a slight male predominance {16731193; 20834239}. Occurrence in children is exceptionally rare {26259494; 21600006; 20055684}.

An origin from a putative thymic epithelial cell precursor with minimal corticomedullary differentiation has been proposed {24236644}. An unsupervised cluster analysis of five genomic data platforms suggests that type B3 thymomas are closely related to type B2 thymomas {29438696}. Recurrent gene copy-number alterations are commoner in type B3 thymomas than other thymoma types {12712440; 10880395; 19861435; 17764580}. Recurrent losses of chromosomes 6q25.2-q25.3 and 3p and gains of chromosome 1q are found in both type B2 and B3 thymomas, while losses of 13q, 16q, and 17p and gains of 4p and 17q are found only in type B3 thymomas and thymic carcinomas {12712440; 10880395; 19861435; 23577124; 22825469}. KMT2A-MAML2 gene fusion has been detected in 6% of cases {32923872}. Copy-number gain of BCL2 and copy-number loss of CDKN2A/B are associated with a poor outcome {22825469}. Inactivating TP53 mutations {29438696} and microsatellite instability {12839963} are rare. While there are no activating mutations in the EGFR gene {29438696; 16919868; 19861435} or KIT gene {29438696; 19861435; 22594902}, genes in the EGFR (HER1) pathway (PIK3CA, AKT1) are rarely mutated {31179560}. Hotspot mutation of GTF2I (p.L424H) is reported in 10–21% of cases {29438696; 28676218; 24974848}.

The tumours usually appear poorly circumscribed, with smooth extensions into mediastinal fat or adjacent organs. Mean diameters range from 51 to 68 mm {12459627; 12239030}. The cut surface is firm and grey or yellow, with tumour nodules separated by fibrous bands. Necrosis and haemorrhage may be present {22338057; 1727679}.

Type B3 thymoma comprises variably sized and shaped lobules delineated by fibrous septa, and it often shows smooth invasive fronts. At low power, the tumour appears pink in H&E-stained slides due to the abundance of polygonal tumour cells that show eosinophilic or clear cytoplasm and form sheets. Intercellular bridges between tumour cells are absent except in rare Hassall corpuscles or squamous eddies. The mildly to moderately atypical, round to elongated, sometimes grooved or raisinoid nuclei can be smaller or larger than those of type B2 thymoma. Nucleoli may be inconspicuous or prominent. Perivascular spaces with epithelial palisading are prominent. Sparse immature T cells are almost always interspersed among the tumour cells, although they may be missing in < 5% of cases. Lymphoid follicles in association with perivascular spaces are common in cases associated with myasthenia gravis.

Thymomas comprising type B3 and B2 components are common (2–16% of all thymomas) and may exceed the frequency of pure type B3 thymomas {12124843; 15084623; 18068351}. Combined thymic carcinomas with a type B3 thymoma component are rare (0.2–1% of thymic epithelial tumours) {15084623; 18068351}.

Immunohistochemistry

The tumour cells usually stain with pancytokeratin antibodies, as well as antibodies to CK19, CK5/6, CK7, CK8, and CK10 but not to CK20. p40 and p63 are almost always positive {12851817; 19369629; 17276940; 25979154}. Focal expression of EMA {1394038} is typical. PAX8 is often positive using polyclonal antibody {21836478}, but negative using monoclonal antibody {24592933}. TTF1, CD20, and thymic carcinoma markers (CD5, KIT [CD117], EZH2) are almost always negative {14762710; 19648882; 29487009} or only focally expressed (GLUT1 and EMA [MUC1]) {19648882; 20625125}. TdT labels low numbers of immature T cells in > 95% of cases.

Rare features in type B3 thymoma

Spindle cells can occur focally in an otherwise typical B3 thymoma. Whether a pure spindle cell subtype of type B3 thymoma exists is unclear, and distinction from atypical type A thymoma is difficult.

Rare type B3 thymomas exhibit anaplasia characterized by the presence of bizarre or giant tumour cells. In contrast to thymic carcinomas, such tumours maintain typical thymoma features such as lobular growth pattern, perivascular spaces, and presence of TdT-positive T cells, and they lack CD5 and KIT (CD117) expression in tumour cells.

Rare tumours showing typical histological features of type B3 thymomas but either exhibiting (usually focal) expression of CD5 or KIT (CD117) {23801129; 16002927} or lacking TdT-positive T cells should still be classified as type B3 thymomas.

Differential diagnosis

Type B2 thymomas are lymphocyte-rich tumours, appearing blue rather than pink in H&E-stained sections. However, because there is a morphological continuum between type B2 and B3 thymomas, rare cases at the B2/B3 boundary may defy clear-cut classification {16711400; 23229995}.

Thymic squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is distinguished from type B3 thymoma by the absence of a lobular growth, infiltrative rather than pushing-type invasion, lack of perivascular spaces, more-prominent nuclear atypia, and frequent presence of intercellular bridges. Thymic SCCs commonly express CD5 (in ~75% of cases), as well as KIT (CD117) and EZH2 (each in > 80%), whereas B3 thymomas do not {14762710; 19648882; 29487009}, with rare exceptions {26893849; 23801129}. CD205 is more frequently positive in thymic SCC than in type B3 thymomas {29487009; 17592270}. GLUT1 expression is more common in thymic SCC (in > 90% of cases) than in type B3 thymomas (~50%) {14762710; 19648882; 20625125; 23801129}; staining is typically diffuse in thymic SCC but patchy in B3 thymoma {26534878}. The cortical epithelial cell marker beta5t may be positive in B3 thymomas but is typically negative in thymic SCC {21836487}. With rare exceptions, TdT-positive immature T cells are absent in thymic SCC {21044186}.
Smears show sheets of tumour cells with some size variation, round nuclei and inconspicuous nucleoli, and rare admixed lymphocytes {20859120}.

Essential:

  • Lobulated tumour
  • Sheets of mildly/moderately atypical, polygonal tumour cells
  • Interspersed perivascular spaces
  • Paucity of lymphocytes

Desirable:

  • TdT immunostain to highlight the small population of immature T cells

Type B3 thymomas should be staged according to the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) TNM system [[Brierley JD, Gospodarowicz MK, Wittekind C, editors. TNM classification of malignant tumours. 8th ed. Oxford (UK): Wiley-Blackwell; 2017.]] {25396314} and, optionally, the Masaoka–Koga system {21847052}.

In the ITMIG cohort {25616178} and an independent meta-analysis (see #14398Table 5.01), 43–55% of type B3 thymomas are in TNM stage I (i.e. Masaoka–Koga stages I and II), while pleural and distant metastasis occurs in 14–15% and 3–5%, respectively.

The reported 5-year, 10-year, and 20-year overall survival rates are 60–86%, 50–70%, and 25–36%, respectively {12124843; 11857293; 15084623; 23154559}. In the ITMIG cohort, the overall survival rates with R0-resected type B3 thymoma at 5 years and 10 years were 89% and 81%, respectively. Complete resection rates range from 53% to 92% {15084623; 12459627; 11857293}. Recurrence occurs in as many as 44% of cases overall {15084623}. After an R0 resection, recurrences occur in 23% and 29% of cases across all tumour stages within 5 years and 10 years, respectively (11% for Masaoka–Koga stage I/II and 28% for stage III within 10 years) {25616178}. Advanced Masaoka–Koga stage (III/IV) is a poor prognostic factor for tumour-related death {15084623}. The prognostic significance of resection status, tumour size, and recurrence has not been reported for single WHO thymoma types, including type B3 thymomas {15111216; 21847050; 12459627; 11857293; 18068351}. Age, sex, and myasthenia gravis have no effect on prognosis {29191778; 25819383; 15084623; 11857293; 8033040}. High PDL1 expression in type B3 thymoma cells is correlated with better overall survival in some studies {31827799; 28771603} but not others {30312607; 28281549; 26794891; 25799277; 25402569}. PDL1 expression levels are a poor predictor of the response to immune checkpoint inhibitor therapies {31608320}.
